bibl.title: On the Working of the Impulses That Appear in the Mind in the Time of Prayer
ܥܠ ܡܥܒܕܢܘܬܐ ܕܙܘܥܐ ܕܒܥܕܢ ܨܠܘܬܐ ܒܗܘܢܐ ܕܢܝܚܢ
bibl.author: Joseph Hazzaya — ܝܘܣܦ ܚܙܝܐ

noteGrp.note: An eighth-century East-Syriac monastic and mystical work by Joseph Hazzaya, transmitted under the name of his brother ʿAbdishoʿ Hazzaya. The work examines the different impulses arising in the mind during prayer and distinguishes them as material, immaterial, and uncircumscribed. It describes the mind’s ascent from sensory and material impulses through spiritual knowledge and contemplation to an imageless ecstasy in the light of the Holy Trinity.

note.quote: ܥܠ ܡܥܒܕܢܘܬܐ ܕܙܘܥܐ ܕܒܥܕܢ ܨܠܘܬܐ ܒܗܘܢܐ ܕܢܝܚܢ. ܕܐܝܠܝܢ ܐܝܬܝܗܘܢ ܡܪܟܒܐ ܐܘܝܠܝܢ ܦܫܝܛܐ. ܘܐܝܠܝܢ ܕܠܐ ܣܟܐ ܘܕܡܘܬܐ. ܩܥܕܢ ܨܠܡܬܐ ܡܢ ܕܡܝܐ ܢܦܫܐ: ܠܐܠܦܐ ܕܩܝܡܐ ܒܠܒܗ ܕܝܡܐ. ܗܘܢܐ ܕܝܢ ܒܕܡܘܬ ܩܘܒܘܢܝܛܐ ܩܐܡ ܥܠ ܐܠܦܐ. ܙܘܥܐ ܕܝܢ ܕܠܐܠܦܐ ܡܕܒܪܝܢ ܐܝܟ ܪܘܚܐ.

On the working of the impulses that appear in the mind in the time of prayer: which of them are material and which are immaterial, and which of them are uncircumscribed and have no form. In the time of prayer the soul resembles a ship standing in the middle of the sea, and the mind stands over the ship like a captain, and the impulses direct the ship like the winds.
ܕܗܘ ܒܚܢܢܗ ܢܫܘܐ ܠܟܠܢ ܠܚܙܬܗ ܫܒܝܚܬܐ: ܗܪܟܐ ܡܢ ܪܗܒܘܢܐܝܬ ܘܬܡܢ ܒܫܪܪܐ ܐܡܝܢ:
May He, by His grace, render all of us worthy of His glorious vision, here as an earnest and there in reality! Amen.
